questions.prompt: What is the core aim of deterrence in this chapter?
choices: Win the conflict after it starts
Make the opponent decide not to attack in the first place
Hide your intentions until after the attack

explanation.gentle: The chapter is about prevention before contact.
explanation.direct: Start with the main goal: make the move look too costly to begin.
explanation.competitive: Deterrence wins by killing the attack in planning.

questions.prompt: Why does Greene insist deterrence is not bluff?
choices: Because visible threat without backing collapses when tested
Because bluffing is only illegal in formal negotiation
Because opponents never pay attention to visible signals

explanation.gentle: A threat has to connect to real capacity.
explanation.direct: Notice the anti-bluff rule: empty display breaks the whole strategy.
explanation.competitive: A fake line gets exposed and cheapens every future warning.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main reversal about overusing deterrence?
choices: Deterrence only works in school settings
Deterrence always invites admiration
Deterrence can make an operator too static and defensive

explanation.gentle: Protective posture can become too permanent.
explanation.direct: The limit is seasonality: hold mode can turn into stagnation.
explanation.competitive: A shield can preserve the present and still kill expansion.

questions.prompt: Helena wants rivals to stop testing her segment. Which move fits the chapter best?
choices: Threaten responses she cannot sustain so the market gets nervous
Choose a few lines to defend and back them with fast, believable enforcement
Ignore the tests until one becomes severe

explanation.gentle: Helena needs credible cost, not louder language.
explanation.direct: Helena improves deterrence by narrowing lines and strengthening backing.
explanation.competitive: Few real punishments beat many fake warnings.

questions.prompt: Micah wants students to stop bending shared equipment rules. What changes behavior before the next violation?
choices: A harsher speech from student leads
A promise to discuss the issue later
A transparent process tied to real, enforceable loss of access

explanation.gentle: Micah needs believable consequence rather than stronger tone.
explanation.direct: The lab example works because process makes cost real and predictable.
explanation.competitive: Turn the rule into price and testing drops fast.

questions.prompt: Tobin can only defend a few boundaries well. What should he do?
choices: Promise to fight every small encroachment
Say nothing about boundaries at all
Defend fewer lines but make those responses highly credible

explanation.gentle: Tobin gains more from credibility than from breadth.
explanation.direct: A narrow believable edge is stronger than a wide symbolic one.
explanation.competitive: Cut the bluff surface and harden the real edge.

questions.prompt: Arielle keeps calling a clause nonnegotiable, but waives it late. What is the better deterrent move?
choices: Keep using the same language until the room respects it
Align the warning with the line she will truly enforce under pressure
Add more dramatic rhetoric around the clause

explanation.gentle: The room needs proof, not repetition.
explanation.direct: The deterrent improves when statement and actual enforcement match.
explanation.competitive: If the line is real, enforce it. If not, stop advertising it.

questions.prompt: Why does inconsistent enforcement damage deterrence so badly?
choices: Because it teaches observers the visible line is negotiable
Because it always saves money in the short run
Because consistency only matters in legal settings

explanation.direct: Inconsistency lowers expected cost and invites testing.
explanation.competitive: One waiver can cheapen the whole wall.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main ethical danger in using deterrence badly?
choices: Deterrence can slide into intimidation theater without real backing
Deterrence always prevents collaboration
Deterrence removes all uncertainty from strategy

explanation.gentle: The danger appears when visible hardness outruns real capacity.
explanation.direct: Ethically, the warning is against projecting force you cannot honestly back.
explanation.competitive: Fake menace is manipulation first and strategy second.

questions.prompt: When would Chapter 11's nonengagement logic be better than Chapter 10's deterrence logic?
choices: When you want to sound more formidable in public
When holding firm is no longer enough and a stronger opponent requires trading space for time
When you have already made the attack look too expensive

explanation.gentle: The next chapter fits moments when yielding ground protects the larger campaign.
explanation.direct: Nonengagement is better when preservation requires space and time rather than visible firmness.
explanation.competitive: If you cannot price them out, you may need to give ground and survive.
